lesenParts.instruction: Read the text(s) and answer the questions in Part 1.

items.signText: Sam, I'm at the shopping centre. The shoe shop you mentioned has closed down, but SportZone next to the cinema has a sale on trainers. Shall I buy the blue pair in your size now, or would you rather choose yourself on Saturday? Mum
items.question: Why is Sam's mum sending this message?
options: a) To find out where the shoe shop has moved to
b) To arrange to meet Sam at the cinema on Saturday
c) To ask if Sam wants her to buy some trainers today
items.explanation: Mum asks 'Shall I buy the blue pair in your size now, or would you rather choose yourself on Saturday?', so she wants to know if she should buy the trainers today. The shoe shop 'has closed down'; it has not moved. The cinema is only mentioned to say where SportZone is, and Saturday is when Sam might choose the shoes, not a meeting at the cinema.

items.signText:
CAR PARK
The first two hours are free if you show a receipt from any shop in the centre at the pay machine before you leave. Without a receipt, the normal charge of £2 per hour applies.
items.question: What does the sign say?
options: a) Parking is free for two hours with a shop receipt.
b) Anyone can park in the car park for two hours without paying.
c) Drivers have to pay at the machine as soon as they arrive.
items.explanation: The first two hours are free 'if you show a receipt from any shop in the centre', so only people who have bought something park for free. Without a receipt 'the normal charge of £2 per hour applies', so parking is not free for everyone, and the receipt is shown at the machine 'before you leave', not on arrival.

items.signText: Our bread is baked in store every morning. Anything left on the shelf at 6 p.m. is reduced to half price. Please note that reduced items cannot be put aside for customers to collect later.
items.question: What does the label tell customers?
options: a) The bread is baked fresh in the store twice a day.
b) Bread still on the shelf in the evening costs less.
c) Staff can keep cheaper bread for you to pick up later.
items.explanation: The label says 'Anything left on the shelf at 6 p.m. is reduced to half price', so bread bought in the evening is cheaper. Reduced items 'cannot be put aside for customers to collect later', so staff will not keep them for you, and the bread is baked 'every morning', not twice a day.

items.signText:
SELF-SERVICE TILLS 1–6: CARD PAYMENTS ONLY.
If you wish to pay with cash, please use the staffed tills near the main entrance. Staff at the customer desk can help with gift vouchers.
items.question: What does the notice say?
options: a) The self-service tills do not accept payment by card.
b) Customers paying with cash should go to the customer desk.
c) Customers who want to pay in cash must use a different till.
items.explanation: The notice says the self-service tills take 'card payments only' and that people who 'wish to pay with cash' should 'use the staffed tills near the main entrance', so cash customers need a different till. The customer desk is only mentioned for gift vouchers, not cash, and the self-service tills do accept cards — in fact they accept only cards.

items.signText:
TROLLEYS
You need a £1 coin to release a trolley. Your coin comes back when you return the trolley to any trolley park. Please do not take trolleys out of the car park.
items.question: What does the sign say about trolleys?
options: a) You may take a trolley home if you leave £1.
b) You will get your money back when you return the trolley.
c) You must return the trolley to the place where you got it.
items.explanation: The sign says 'Your coin comes back when you return the trolley', so you get your £1 back. Trolleys must not be taken 'out of the car park', so you cannot take one home, and you can return it 'to any trolley park', not only the one where you got it.

questions.question: Laura would like to learn to take better photos, but she only has a mobile phone. She works every Saturday, and she would like someone to comment on her pictures after the course has finished.
questions.explanation: Photos with Your Phone is on Sunday, teaches people to use 'the camera on their mobile phone', and 'after the course, you can send your photos to the teacher by email and get personal advice'. Street Photography Day is also about photos, but it is on Saturday, when Laura works, and you must 'bring your own digital camera, as phones are not suitable'.
options: A
B
C
D
E
F
G
H

questions.question: Tom has hardly ever cooked, and he would like to learn together with his twelve-year-old daughter. They are only free on Saturday mornings.
questions.explanation: Kitchen Basics is 'for families to learn together', accepts 'children aged ten and over' with an adult, is for people who have 'never cooked before' and takes place on Saturday morning. A Taste of Italy is also a cooking class, but it is on Sunday afternoon and is for people who 'already feel confident in the kitchen'.
options: A
B
C
D
E
F
G
H

questions.question: Maria has been cooking for years and wants to learn to make dishes from another country. She doesn't eat meat, and she prefers learning in a small group where the teacher has time for everyone.
questions.explanation: A Taste of Italy is for people who 'already feel confident in the kitchen', teaches 'real Italian home cooking', has 'no more than eight students' so 'everyone gets plenty of attention', and 'several dishes are made without meat'. Kitchen Basics is also about cooking, but it is for people who have 'never cooked before' and does not teach food from another country.
options: A
B
C
D
E
F
G
H

questions.question: James wants to try painting for the first time and doesn't own any equipment. He would like to spend the whole weekend outside, and he enjoys walking.
questions.explanation: Painting in the Hills is a 'two-day course' that 'takes place entirely outdoors', includes a walk of 'about three kilometres' each morning, needs 'no experience', and 'all paints, brushes and paper are provided'. Pottery Weekend also lasts two days, needs no experience and provides everything, but it is held 'in our bright studio', not outside, and it is not painting.
options: A
B
C
D
E
F
G
H

questions.question: Sophie loves writing and wants to improve her stories. She has a young baby, so she can't leave the house, and she would love to see her writing printed one day.
questions.explanation: The Home Story Club can be done 'from your own home' by video call, is about 'short stories', and 'the best stories are printed in a small book'. Write Your Own Songs is also a writing course, but it is held at the Riverside Arts Centre, so Sophie would have to leave the house, and the songs are performed, not printed.
options: A
B
C

G

lesenParts.instruction: Read the text(s) and answer the questions in Part 3.
lesenParts.textTitle: My summer with the sea turtles
lesenParts.text:
When I finished school last year, most of my friends went straight to university. I wasn't sure what I wanted to study, so I decided to spend three months as a volunteer on a sea turtle project on a small Greek island. My parents weren't very keen at first. They thought I should get a job and save money instead, but when I showed them that the organisation had been running for over twenty years, they began to feel more relaxed about it.

I arrived in June, just as the turtles were starting to lay their eggs on the beaches. There were about fifteen volunteers from all over the world, and we lived together at a simple campsite with tents and a shared kitchen. I'd never been camping before, and I'll be honest: the first week was hard. It was extremely hot, there were insects everywhere and I missed having my own room. But I soon got used to it, and by the end I actually preferred sleeping outside.

Our main job was to walk along the beaches early in the morning, looking for the tracks the turtles had left in the sand during the night. When we found a nest, we protected it with a metal cage so that dogs and foxes couldn't dig up the eggs. We also put up signs asking tourists not to use umbrellas or chairs near the nests. Most visitors were very interested and asked lots of questions, although a few were annoyed that part of the beach was closed.

What surprised me most was how much time we spent talking to people. Every evening, two volunteers ran an information stand in the harbour. I was terrified the first time because my Greek was limited to 'hello' and 'thank you', and many of the visitors were Greek families. However, the other volunteers helped me, and I learnt enough phrases to explain the basics. By August I was confident enough to give short talks to groups of children, which is something I would never have imagined doing a year earlier.

The best moment came near the end of my stay, when the first eggs hatched. Watching dozens of tiny turtles run across the sand towards the sea at midnight is something I will never forget. Only about one in a thousand will survive to become an adult, which made me realise why the project's work matters so much.

Looking back, I think the experience taught me more than any classroom could. I've now decided to study marine biology, and I'm hoping to return to the island next summer as a team leader. If you're thinking of volunteering, my advice is simple: don't choose a project just because it looks good in photos. Find out exactly what the work involves, and make sure it's something you really care about.

questions.question: Why did the writer's parents begin to feel better about her plan?
questions.explanation: The writer says that 'when I showed them that the organisation had been running for over twenty years, they began to feel more relaxed about it'. Her parents wanted her to 'get a job and save money instead', but she never promises to do this, and her friends 'went straight to university', not to the project.
options: a) Several of her friends were going on the same project.
b) She promised to find a job when she came back.
c) She had already saved enough money for the trip.
d) They learnt that the organisation had a long history.

questions.question: How did the writer feel about living at the campsite?
questions.explanation: She says 'the first week was hard', but 'I soon got used to it, and by the end I actually preferred sleeping outside'. She had 'never been camping before', so she was not camping again, and she says she soon got used to the conditions, so she did not miss her own room for the whole stay.
options: a) She never really got used to the heat and the insects.
b) She wished she had had her own room for the whole stay.
c) She found it difficult at first but later came to enjoy it.
d) She was pleased to be camping again after many years.

questions.question: What does the writer say about the tourists on the beaches?
questions.explanation: The writer says 'Most visitors were very interested and asked lots of questions'. Only 'a few were annoyed that part of the beach was closed', not most of them, and she never says that tourists damaged nests or ignored the signs.
options: a) Many of them wanted to find out more about the turtles.
b) Most of them were unhappy that some of the beach was closed.
c) They often damaged the nests with their chairs and umbrellas.
d) Very few of them paid attention to the volunteers' signs.

questions.question: Why was the writer frightened the first time she worked at the information stand?
questions.explanation: She was 'terrified the first time because my Greek was limited to "hello" and "thank you"'. She only gave talks to children later, 'by August', and 'the other volunteers helped me', so she was not left alone.
options: a) She had to give a talk to a large group of children.
b) The other volunteers had left her there on her own.
c) She did not know enough facts about sea turtles.
d) She could only say a few words in the local language.

questions.question: What advice does the writer give to people who are thinking of volunteering?
questions.explanation: Her advice is to 'Find out exactly what the work involves, and make sure it's something you really care about'. She warns people not to choose a project 'just because it looks good in photos', and she does not advise learning the language first or going with a friend.
options: a) Learn some of the local language before you leave.
b) Check carefully what you will be expected to do.
c) Go with a friend so that you do not feel lonely.
d) Choose a project in a place that looks beautiful.

lesenParts.instruction: Read the text(s) and answer the questions in Part 4.
lesenParts.text:
Twenty years ago, learning a new language or studying for a qualification usually meant sitting in a classroom at a fixed time each week. Today, millions of people learn at their kitchen table, on the bus or even in bed. (1) ______ In some countries, more than half of all adults have now taken at least one course on the internet.

There are several reasons for this growth. The most obvious is that the internet has become faster and cheaper, so watching video lessons is no longer a problem for most people. (2) ______ For example, a nurse who works nights can study during the day, while a parent can wait until the children are asleep.

Universities have also played a part. Many of them now put recordings of their lectures on the internet. (3) ______ Some of these have attracted over a million students, which would be impossible in any lecture hall.

However, online learning is not perfect. Many people sign up for a course with great enthusiasm but never finish it. (4) ______ Without a teacher checking their progress, they find it easy to put off the next lesson until tomorrow, and then the day after.

To solve this problem, many course designers now include ways for learners to stay in touch with each other. (5) ______ Students who feel part of a group, it seems, are much more likely to reach the end. In the future, the best courses may combine the freedom of learning online with the support that classrooms have always provided.

questions.question: Choose the sentence that best fits gap (1).
questions.explanation: 'Learning in this way' refers back to learning 'at their kitchen table, on the bus or even in bed', and the idea that it 'has become completely normal' is supported by the next sentence: 'more than half of all adults have now taken at least one course on the internet'. The sentence about printed textbooks is about paper books, so it breaks the link between these two sentences.
options: A) Some go even further and offer complete courses that anyone can join for free.
B) As a result, most online courses now cost more than they did ten years ago.
C) Learning in this way, once unusual, has become completely normal.
D) These include discussion forums, weekly video meetings and online study partners.
E) Because of this, schools no longer need to employ as many teachers.
F) Another reason is that online students can decide for themselves when to study.
G) Printed textbooks, however, are still more popular than ever.
H) Research suggests that the main reason is a lack of motivation.

questions.question: Choose the sentence that best fits gap (2).
questions.explanation: The paragraph begins 'There are several reasons for this growth. The most obvious is ...', so 'Another reason' continues the list. The idea that students 'decide for themselves when to study' is then explained by the example of the nurse who 'can study during the day' and the parent who waits 'until the children are asleep'. The sentence saying courses 'cost more' contradicts 'faster and cheaper', and the one about schools needing fewer teachers is not what the nurse example shows.
options: A) Some go even further and offer complete courses that anyone can join for free.
B) As a result, most online courses now cost more than they did ten years ago.
C) Learning in this way, once unusual, has become completely normal.
D) These include discussion forums, weekly video meetings and online study partners.
E) Because of this, schools no longer need to employ as many teachers.
F) Another reason is that online students can decide for themselves when to study.
G) Printed textbooks, however, are still more popular than ever.
H) Research suggests that the main reason is a lack of motivation.

questions.question: Choose the sentence that best fits gap (3).
questions.explanation: 'Some go even further' refers to the universities that put 'recordings of their lectures on the internet', and adds a bigger step: 'complete courses that anyone can join for free'. The next sentence, 'Some of these have attracted over a million students', needs these free courses as its subject. Printed textbooks do not attract 'students' in a lecture hall, so that sentence cannot fit.
options: A) Some go even further and offer complete courses that anyone can join for free.
B) As a result, most online courses now cost more than they did ten years ago.
C) Learning in this way, once unusual, has become completely normal.
D) These include discussion forums, weekly video meetings and online study partners.
E) Because of this, schools no longer need to employ as many teachers.
F) Another reason is that online students can decide for themselves when to study.
G) Printed textbooks, however, are still more popular than ever.
H) Research suggests that the main reason is a lack of motivation.

questions.question: Choose the sentence that best fits gap (4).
questions.explanation: 'The main reason' explains why many people 'never finish' their course, and 'a lack of motivation' is then described in the next sentence: without a teacher, 'they find it easy to put off the next lesson'. The sentence about schools employing fewer teachers does not explain why people stop studying.
options: A) Some go even further and offer complete courses that anyone can join for free.
B) As a result, most online courses now cost more than they did ten years ago.
C) Learning in this way, once unusual, has become completely normal.
D) These include discussion forums, weekly video meetings and online study partners.
E) Because of this, schools no longer need to employ as many teachers.
F) Another reason is that online students can decide for themselves when to study.
G) Printed textbooks, however, are still more popular than ever.
H) Research suggests that the main reason is a lack of motivation.

questions.question: Choose the sentence that best fits gap (5).
questions.explanation: 'These' refers to the 'ways for learners to stay in touch with each other', and the sentence gives examples: 'discussion forums, weekly video meetings and online study partners'. The following sentence about students who 'feel part of a group' continues this idea. The sentence about online courses costing more has no link to staying in touch.
options: A) Some go even further and offer complete courses that anyone can join for free.
B) As a result, most online courses now cost more than they did ten years ago.
C) Learning in this way, once unusual, has become completely normal.
D) These include discussion forums, weekly video meetings and online study partners.
E) Because of this, schools no longer need to employ as many teachers.
F) Another reason is that online students can decide for themselves when to study.
G) Printed textbooks, however, are still more popular than ever.
H) Research suggests that the main reason is a lack of motivation.

lesenParts.instruction: Read the text(s) and answer the questions in Part 5.
lesenParts.text:
Last spring, our class went on a five-day trip to the mountains in Wales. We (1) ______ at a youth hostel in a small village, and every day our teachers organised a different activity. On the first morning we went climbing. I had never done it before, and at first I was too nervous to (2) ______ down, but our instructor was very patient. By lunchtime I had reached the top of the wall twice!

The next day we went on a long walk to a lake. The weather (3) ______ suddenly in the afternoon, and we got completely wet (4) ______ the way back. Luckily, the hostel staff had made hot soup for us, which warmed us up in no time.

In the evenings we played games and told stories. My best friend Leo, who is usually quite shy, (5) ______ everyone laugh with his funny impressions of our teachers. Fortunately, the teachers found them funny too!

I learnt a lot on the trip, not only about the mountains but also about working in a team. I would definitely (6) ______ it to next year's students.

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (1).
questions.explanation: 'We stayed at a youth hostel' is the normal way to say where you slept during a trip. 'Put', 'kept' and 'spent' all need an object (you put or keep something; you spend time or money), so 'We put/kept/spent at a youth hostel' is not correct.
options: a) put
b) kept
c) stayed
d) spent

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (2).
questions.explanation: When you point your eyes in a direction, the verb is 'look': 'too nervous to look down'. 'See', 'watch' and 'view' are not used with 'down' in this way.
options: a) watch
b) look
c) view
d) see

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (3).
questions.explanation: 'The weather changed suddenly' makes sense, and it explains why they 'got completely wet'. 'Became' and 'went' need a word after them (became cold, went grey), and weather does not 'move'.
options: a) changed
b) went
c) moved
d) became

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (4).
questions.explanation: The fixed phrase is 'on the way back', meaning during the journey back to the hostel. 'In the way' has a different meaning (blocking someone), and 'at the way' and 'by the way' do not mean 'during the journey'.
options: a) at
b) by
c) in
d) on

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (5).
questions.explanation: The structure is 'make someone do something': Leo 'made everyone laugh'. 'Caused' and 'got' need 'to' before the verb (caused/got everyone to laugh), and 'did everyone laugh' is not correct here.
options: a) made
b) did
c) caused
d) got

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (6).
questions.explanation: You 'recommend something to someone' when you say it is good: 'I would definitely recommend it to next year's students'. We 'advise' and 'persuade' people, not things ('advise it to' and 'persuade it to' are wrong), and 'tell it to' would mean repeating a story.
options: a) advise
b) recommend
c) tell
d) persuade

lesenParts.instruction: Read the text(s) and answer the questions in Part 6.
lesenParts.textTitle: My summer as a camp leader
lesenParts.text:
Last summer I worked as a group leader at an adventure camp for teenagers in Scotland, and it was the best job I have (1) ______ had. I was responsible (2) ______ a group of twelve children aged between eleven and fourteen. Every morning I had to wake them up, make sure they ate a good breakfast and then take them to their activities, most (3) ______ which were outdoors. We went kayaking on the lake, climbed rocks and learnt how to build a fire safely.

The days were long and tiring. Some evenings I was (4) ______ exhausted that I fell asleep before the children did! The hardest part was looking after the ones who felt homesick. One boy, Callum, cried every night during his first week. I spent a lot of time talking to him and finding games he enjoyed, and by the end of the camp he was (5) ______ of the happiest children there.

I also made some great friends among the other leaders, and we still chat online most weeks. (6) ______ soon as applications open again, I'm going to apply for next summer.

questions.question: Write ONE word to fill gap (1).
questions.explanation: After a superlative with the present perfect we use 'ever': 'the best job I have ever had'. 'Never' would give the opposite meaning and is not possible after 'the best'.

questions.question: Write ONE word to fill gap (2).
questions.explanation: The adjective 'responsible' is always followed by 'for': 'I was responsible for a group of twelve children'.

questions.question: Write ONE word to fill gap (3).
questions.explanation: The relative phrase is 'most of which': 'their activities, most of which were outdoors', meaning that most of the activities took place outside.

questions.question: Write ONE word to fill gap (4).
questions.explanation: The structure 'so + adjective + that' shows a result: 'I was so exhausted that I fell asleep before the children did'. 'Such' is used before a noun, not an adjective alone, and 'too' cannot be followed by 'that'.

questions.question: Write ONE word to fill gap (5).
questions.explanation: 'One of the' is followed by a superlative and a plural noun: 'one of the happiest children'. By the end of the camp Callum was very happy, which contrasts with how he cried every night in his first week.

questions.question: Write ONE word to fill gap (6).
questions.explanation: The time expression is 'as soon as', meaning 'immediately when': 'As soon as applications open again, I'm going to apply'. No other word can come before 'soon as' here.

horenParts.instruction: Listen and answer the questions in Part 1.
horenParts.transcript:
Girl: Hi Sam, it's Maya. It's about tomorrow. I know I said we'd meet at the ticket office, but it's always really crowded there in the morning. I thought about the café, but I've just remembered it's closed on Sundays. So let's meet under the big clock by the main entrance instead. It's easy to find. See you there at nine!

Woman: Hi Tom, it's me. I'm still at the station, and I'm afraid I'm going to be late. My train to York was supposed to leave at ten fifteen, but there's a problem with the signals. At first they said it would leave half an hour late, so at quarter to eleven. But they've just changed it again on the board, and now it says eleven o'clock. So I'll probably get to you around lunchtime. Sorry!

Driver: Good morning, everyone, and welcome aboard this coach to Edinburgh. The journey normally takes three hours, and that includes a short stop at a service station. But I'm afraid there are roadworks near Newcastle today, so we expect to arrive about half an hour later than usual. That means the whole trip will take around three and a half hours. Don't worry, though. Last winter, in the snow, it took us over four hours!

Woman: So, did you pack everything for your trip?
Man: I thought so. I checked my passport about three times, and I remembered to put my phone charger in at the last minute. But guess what? I left my sunglasses on the kitchen table! And it's supposed to be sunny all week.
Woman: Oh dear. Well, you can always buy some at the airport.
Man: I suppose so, but they're so expensive there.

Woman: A single to Cambridge, please.
Man: That's twelve pounds. Are you coming back today? Because an off-peak day return is only fourteen.
Woman: Oh, yes, I'm coming back this evening.
Man: Then the return is much better value. We also sell a weekly pass, but that's only worth it if you're travelling every day.
Woman: No, it's just today. I'll take the return, then.

Man: So how are you getting to the airport on Friday?
Woman: Well, I was going to take the bus because it's the cheapest, but it takes nearly two hours with all the stops. My brother offered to drive me, but his car's at the garage until next week. So in the end I've booked a seat on the train. It's only forty minutes, and the station is right next to the terminal.
Man: Sounds perfect.

Man: Excuse me, is this where the Oxford train goes from? Platform seven?
Woman: Well, it normally leaves from platform seven, but not today. They're doing some building work over there, so it's going from platform three instead.
Man: Three? Do I need to go over the bridge?
Woman: No, it's just past platform five, on this side. You can't miss it.
Man: Great, thanks very much.

questions.question: Where will Maya and Sam meet?
questions.explanation: Maya says "let's meet under the big clock by the main entrance instead". She changes the plan to meet at the ticket office because it is too crowded, and the café is closed on Sundays.
options: a) at a station café
b) under a large clock
c) at a ticket office

questions.question: What time will the woman's train leave?
questions.explanation: The woman says the board has changed again: "now it says eleven o'clock". Ten fifteen was the original time, and quarter to eleven was the first new time, which was then changed.
options: a) a station clock showing 10.45
b) a station clock showing 11.00
c) a station clock showing 10.15

Don't worry, though. Last winter, in the snow, it took us over four hours!

questions.question: How long will the coach journey take today?
questions.explanation: The driver says that because of roadworks "the whole trip will take around three and a half hours". Three hours is the normal time, and four hours was how long it took last winter in the snow.
options: a) a clock face showing four hours
b) a clock face showing three hours
c) a clock face showing three and a half hours

Woman: Oh dear. Well, you can always buy some at the airport.
Man: I suppose so, but they're so expensive there.

questions.question: What did the man forget to pack?
questions.explanation: The man says "I left my sunglasses on the kitchen table". He checked his passport three times and remembered to put his phone charger in, so he has both of those.
options: a) a passport
b) a phone charger
c) a pair of sunglasses

questions.question: What kind of ticket does the woman buy?
questions.explanation: She first asks for a single, but when she hears the return costs only two pounds more and she is coming back that evening, she says "I'll take the return, then". The weekly pass is only worth it for daily travel, so she does not want it.
options: a) a single ticket

Girl: Hi, Ben, it's Lucy. It's about tonight.
Boy: Hi, Lucy. Is everything OK?
Girl: Yes, but you know we were going to see the film at seven? I have to help my mum in the shop after work, so could we go to the nine o'clock one instead? Oh, and don't worry about your bike. My brother fixed mine yesterday, so I don't need to borrow it any more.
Boy: Nine's fine with me. See you at the cinema.

Boy: Are you coming on the trip to the science museum on Friday?
Girl: I have to. It's part of the course. I don't mind museums, and science is one of my favourite subjects, so that's not the problem.
Boy: Is it the early start? The coach leaves at seven.
Girl: No, that's fine. It's just that they've chosen the day of my swimming final. I've been training for months, and now I'm going to miss it. It's so unfair. Why couldn't they pick another day?

Man: Did you finish that crime series you were watching?
Woman: No, I stopped after four episodes.
Man: Oh? I thought the actors were supposed to be really good.
Woman: They were. The woman who played the detective was brilliant. And it wasn't about time. I was on holiday, so I had plenty of it. But there were so many characters, and it kept jumping backwards and forwards in time. By episode four, I had no idea what was going on, so I gave up.

Man: Is that your new phone? What do you think of it?
Woman: Well, it cost less than I expected because it was in the sale. And it's really simple to use. I set it up in five minutes. But the photos are nothing like the ones in the adverts. In the evening, they all come out dark and blurry.
Man: That's a shame. The camera was the main reason you chose it.
Woman: Exactly. I feel a bit let down, to be honest.

Woman: Have you been to that new café on Market Street yet?
Man: Yes, I went on Saturday with my sister. The cakes were lovely, and to be honest, the prices weren't bad for the size of them.
Woman: I heard it gets really busy.
Man: It was full, but they keep the music quiet, so we could chat easily. The problem was that we waited forty minutes for two coffees. There were only two people working there. I won't go back until they've got more staff.

Man: Since I started cycling to work, I feel so much fitter.
Woman: Me too. I sleep better, and I've got loads more energy. I'm not sure it saves me any money, though. I spent a fortune on the bike and all the clothes.
Man: Really? I think I save loads on petrol.
Woman: Maybe. And for me it's slower than the car. It takes me twice as long.
Man: Not for me. The traffic on my road is terrible in the mornings, so I get there much faster on my bike.

horenParts.instruction: Listen and answer the questions in Part 3.
horenParts.transcript:
Coach: Good evening, everyone, and thanks for staying behind after training. I've got some exciting news about the club. As you know, we've been raising money for something new for over a year. A lot of you were hoping for a swimming pool, but I'm afraid that was far too expensive. Instead, we've built an indoor climbing wall, and it's ready to use from next week.

Now, if you've never climbed before, don't worry. We're running beginners' classes. We originally planned to have them on Tuesday evenings, but the hall is already busy then, so they'll be on Thursday evenings from seven till eight thirty.

What do you need? Well, you don't need to buy special shoes, because the club will lend you a pair, and we'll give you a helmet as well. But please bring your own water bottle. Climbing is hard work, and we can't sell drinks in the hall.

There's also a special offer. Last year new members got a free T-shirt, but this year anyone who joins before the end of May will get a free sports bag with the club logo on it.

To book a place on a class, you'll need to go to reception. We're hoping to add bookings to the website soon, but it isn't working properly yet, so please don't try that for now.

Finally, we need volunteers for July. The summer barbecue is already organised, thanks to the parents' committee, but we still need people to help with the fun run through the park. If you're free, please put your name on the list by the door. Thanks, everyone!

horenParts.instruction: Listen and answer the questions in Part 4.
horenParts.transcript:
Interviewer: Today I'm talking to Helen Price, who works as a ranger in a national park in the north of England. Helen, why did you choose this job?
Helen: People often assume I wanted to escape the city, but actually I loved living in London. And the money certainly isn't the reason anyone becomes a ranger! No, it really goes back to when I was about ten. A ranger took our school group out at night to look for badgers, and I remember thinking, that's what I want to do when I grow up.
Interviewer: What's the hardest part of the job?
Helen: Everyone expects me to say the weather, but I've got good clothes, and I actually enjoy a stormy day. The hours can be long in summer, but I don't mind that either. What I find really difficult is when visitors leave rubbish or let their dogs chase the sheep, even though there are signs everywhere. I'm not comfortable telling people off, but sometimes I have to.
Interviewer: The park has had far more visitors in recent years. How do you feel about that?
Helen: Some of my colleagues worry about the paths getting damaged, but we've repaired most of them now, so I'm not too concerned. And the car parks get busy at weekends, but it's never really crowded up on the hills. Honestly, I'm delighted. So many people have discovered the outdoors, and that can only be a good thing.
Interviewer: Has technology changed your work?
Helen: A lot. We use cameras to count the animals, and there's an app for reporting problems like fallen trees. They save us loads of time, and they don't cost as much as people think. But a camera can't tell you why the deer have moved to a different valley. You still need someone who really knows the land.
Interviewer: What would you say to young people who'd like to do your job?
Helen: A degree can help, but it isn't essential. Some of the best rangers I know never went to university. Some people start by working in visitor centres, which is fine, but you don't learn much about the land there. The best thing is to volunteer. Parks are always looking for helpers, and it's the only way to find out if you really love the work.
Interviewer: And what about your own future?
Helen: I was offered a job training new rangers at our head office, but I turned it down. I'd be sitting at a desk all day. I did once think about working in a national park in Canada, but I'd miss this place too much. No, I'm happy right where I am, and I hope I'll still be here when I retire.

schreibenParts.task:
Read this email from your English-speaking friend Jamie and the notes you have made.

From: Jamie
Subject: My visit!

Hi!

Great news: I've booked my ticket, and I'm coming to stay with you for the weekend next month! [Note 1: Brilliant!]

I'll arrive on Friday evening. Is it better for me to get a taxi from the station to your house, or can you meet me? [Note 2: Explain]

What do you think we should do on Saturday? I'd love to see the best places in your town. [Note 3: Suggest...]

Also, what should I bring? I've no idea what the weather will be like. [Note 4: Tell Jamie]

See you soon,
Jamie

Write your email to Jamie using all the notes. Write about 100 words.

Choose ONE of these questions. Write your answer in about 100 words.

Question A: Article
You see this notice on an English-language website for young people.

Articles wanted!
A day out in my town
Where would you take a visitor for a perfect day out in your town? What would you do there, and why would they enjoy it?
The best articles will be published on our website.

Write your article.

Question B: Story
Your English teacher has asked you to write a story. Your story must begin with this sentence:

When I opened the door, my friend was standing there.

Write your story.

sprechenParts.title: Part 1 — Speaking
sprechenParts.situation:
The examiner asks you some questions about yourself, travel and holidays. Answer each question with two or three sentences.

1. What's your name? Where do you live?
2. How do you usually travel to school or work?
3. Where did you go on your last holiday?
4. Do you prefer holidays by the sea or in the mountains? Why?
5. Tell us about a place in your country that you would like to visit.

sprechenParts.title: Part 2 — Speaking
sprechenParts.situation: Look at the photograph. It shows a family on holiday in a small harbour town by the sea. There are colourful houses along the water, boats in the harbour, and the family is sitting at a table outside a café, looking at a map. Tell us what you can see in the photograph. You have about one minute.

sprechenParts.title: Part 3 — Speaking
sprechenParts.situation:
Your class has won a prize: a one-day trip together. Here are some places you could go.

a city with museums and shops
a beach
a theme park
a national park for walking
a farm where you can help with the animals

Talk together about the different places and say which would be the most fun and interesting for the whole class. Then decide which place is best. You have about two or three minutes.

sprechenParts.title: Part 4 — Speaking
sprechenParts.situation:
The examiner asks you and your partner some more questions about travelling. Give your opinion and reasons, and respond to what your partner says.

1. Do you prefer going on holiday with your family or with friends? Why?
2. Is it better to plan a trip carefully or to decide things when you get there?
3. What was the best trip you have ever been on? What made it special?
4. Do you think people should travel less by plane? Why or why not?
5. What can people learn from visiting other countries?
